- **Bears schedule** — Chicago’s 2026 slate is being framed as tough, but several analysts note it may be more manageable than advertised: SI called it the third-easiest schedule in the NFC North, with a relatively lighter start and seven standalone games. The Bears also drew the third-fewest air miles in the NFL, which should help with travel wear and tear over a long season. [4, 5]

- **Bears schedule** — Chicago has a heavy national spotlight load in 2026, with seven primetime/standalone games including Thanksgiving and Christmas appearances. That kind of exposure reflects the team’s 2025 surge under Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams, and it raises the stakes for how they handle late-game pressure again. [1, 4, 6]

- **Bears vs. NFC North** — The schedule may be difficult, but the bigger takeaway is that Chicago’s rivals are also being weighed against it and may not have a clear edge. SI’s breakdown says the Bears’ slate looks third among NFC North teams, behind Green Bay and Minnesota in scheduling favorability, which matters in a division that could come down to marginal advantages. [4]

- **Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins** — Cincinnati’s 2026 schedule release has fueled optimism that the Bengals can make another AFC Championship run, with the schedule writeup highlighting only four games against 2025 winning teams and pointing to a favorable division setup. The fantasy angle is straightforward: if Burrow stays healthy, the passing-game ceiling remains elite. What to watch next is whether that “favorable” slate actually translates once the season starts. [3]

- **Bengals** — Cincinnati opened as an early Week 1 favorite over Tampa Bay in the “Open in Orange” game, with sportsbooks listing the Bengals anywhere from 2.5 to 3.5 points ahead at home. That suggests the market is buying Cincinnati as the better Week 1 side despite Zac Taylor’s 2-5 record in season openers. [6]

- **Bengals** — The 2026 schedule does not give Cincinnati consecutive home games until Weeks 17 and 18, the latest that has ever happened in franchise history. The team also has back-to-back road stretches in Weeks 2-3 and 15-16, which could affect rhythm and streaks, though the practical fantasy impact is still not specified. [7]

- **Bengals** — Week 16 is one of four candidate games for NFL Network’s late-season Saturday doubleheader, with Bengals-Colts listed as a possible 4:30 p.m. ET or 8:00 p.m. ET slot. That means Cincinnati could get a standalone national window late in the year, but the final assignment is not decided yet. [8]

BUF.summary:
- **Bills schedule** — Buffalo drew a demanding 2026 slate with seven standalone games, two holiday spots, and an eighth-ranked strength of schedule. The key quirks are a first-ever Thanksgiving home game against the Chiefs and a Christmas Day trip to the Broncos, with the toughest stretches landing in Weeks 1-5 and 12-16. That sets up an early-season and late-season grind for a team with high expectations; how the new coaching staff manages the short weeks and marquee showcases will matter. [3, 5]

- **Skyler Bell** — Bell, listed as a Bills wide receiver, was one of the rookies on the field for rookie minicamp and showed early nerves. He had trouble securing the ball cleanly in drills, with a couple of drops during routes-on-air work. That doesn’t settle anything, but it’s the kind of first impression that puts a late-round or depth receiver on the watch list as the rookie class and tryout group compete for roles. [7, 8]

SF.summary:
- **Cornerback room** — Deommodore Lenoir is most likely to remain in the starting lineup, but his role in the slot could shift more under Raheem Morris. Darrell Luter looks pushed off the roster, while Renardo Green is on the hot seat with new competition around him. Hobbs can play inside or outside and could push Stout and Green; Tre’Vius Hodges-Tomlinson, Jones, Prysock, Neal, Robinson and Apple are part of the depth fight, with Neal’s special teams value standing out. [1]

- **Safety room** — Mustapha emerged as the clear top safety in the second half last season and does not appear to be threatened for snaps. Brown has the least competition he has had in his 49ers tenure despite an uneven year, while Sigle looks more like a dime-role contender than a Week 1 starter. The back end is thin enough that UDFA Canteen, Stroman and Worth all have a real path to the roster or practice squad, and McMorris is another depth name to watch. [2]

- **Raheem Morris** — Kyle Shanahan’s new defensive coordinator brings a familiar scheme background, with Shanahan pointing to Morris’s work with the Rams as a useful template. The key takeaway is that Morris has a history of adapting structure while adding his own wrinkles, so the 49ers’ defensive roles in the secondary could be more fluid than before. [5]

- **Bye week timing** — San Francisco’s bye comes right after a Week 7 East Coast game, giving the team an early reset before the second half of the season. The path into the bye is also relatively light on travel beyond the Australia trip and one coast-to-coast swing, which could help the roster stay fresher early. [8]

It’s one of the schedule’s more notable non-divisional checkpoints and could matter for late-season fatigue management, especially with the middle and end of the slate already carrying multiple high-profile matchups. BAL.summary:
- **Ravens schedule** — Baltimore is slated for four primetime games and could get a fifth if the Week 18 finale against Pittsburgh is flexed; the team also won’t play a night game in the first month, which the schedule write-up framed as a “soft launch.” That keeps the early slate lighter, but it also means fewer national-stage fantasy spots for Ravens skill players until later in the season. - **Ravens schedule** — The middle of Baltimore’s schedule looks brutal, with five straight games against playoff teams from last season after the Week 7 Bengals matchup and a Week 13 bye. The stretch includes Buffalo, Jacksonville on a short week, the Chargers after a mini-bye, then road games at Carolina and Houston, so this run will likely define the division race and playoff positioning. [5]

- **Ja’Kobi Lane** — Baltimore’s third-round wide receiver out of USC is being projected as a contested-catch and red-zone weapon after the departures of DeAndre Hopkins and Isaiah Likely. Early on, he’s described as a situational piece with chain-moving and scoring upside while he refines his route running, but the report also notes starting X receiver potential if he develops. [7]

- **Calais Campbell** — Campbell passed his physical and officially signed his one-year deal to return to Baltimore. The reported deal is worth $5.5 million in 2026 with $4.75 million guaranteed, giving the Ravens an experienced interior presence on the defensive front. [8]

The preview notes Corum’s burst and shiftiness, plus his steady weekly carry volume, which supports a bigger role if the Rams keep leaning on a two-back setup. That matters for fantasy because Corum has already shown usable weekly involvement, not just sporadic change-of-pace snaps. [5]

- **Sean McVay / Rams passing-game depth** — The Rams’ receiver depth behind Puka Nacua was exposed when Nacua missed time with an ankle injury, forcing McVay to lean on a thin group behind Davante Adams. Tutu Atwell had not earned a larger role, Jordan Whittington was only a partial stand-in, and Xavier Smith and Konata Mumpfield were later-season depth pieces. That context matters because it shows how fragile the WR rotation can get if injuries hit again. [1]

- **Rams schedule** — Los Angeles will play seven primetime games in 2026, including four in the first five weeks, and opens with the 49ers in Melbourne before getting 11 days before Week 2. The schedule also gets the Rams’ tougher travel out of the way early, including trips to Philadelphia and Denver within the first month. That matters because the early rest structure could help with recovery and injury management while keeping the Rams highly visible in fantasy and betting markets. [4, 8]
